# Accession neighbours are common in Minneapolis. Later rights decisions seldom have one.

Among 59,622 valid training records from December 2024, only 17 had an empty rights declaration. All 17 still had an empty field in January 2026. The interval supplies no training examples for predicting a later fill from earlier accession neighbours. The independent evaluation remains unopened. [Audit protocol and splits](design.md) · [Release counts](feasibility.json)

**Recorded pending decisions give a different result.** Of 1,302 records initially marked “Copyright Not Evaluated” or “Copyright Undetermined,” 57 acquired another declaration. Of those, 54 became “In Copyright,” two became “No Known Copyright,” and one became “Public Domain.” They spanned 12 accession clusters, treating objects without a usable family key as singletons. Only **two of the 57** had any sibling with a substantive declaration already visible in 2024. The observed operational problem therefore gives an accession-neighbour model little information precisely where the institution later recorded decisions. This conclusion is specific to these releases, the training partition and the written definition of a sibling. [Pending-state protocol](pending.md) · [Observed later decisions](pending.json)

**Artificial masking would measure an easier problem.** Of 59,605 objects with an explicit early label, 41,497 (69.62%) belonged to a family with another labelled training object. The nearest such member by object ID agreed on the literal Public Domain indicator for 39,742 (95.77%). This is a descriptive, within-training agreement with no fitted model. Of 4,366 repeated families, 316 contained both label values. One family contributed 1,027 objects, making object-level independence an implausible assumption. These data support a controlled masked-field experiment after the Met method is frozen, with family-clustered uncertainty and a direct nearest-sibling control. The temporal results limit what that experiment could establish about actual metadata repair. [Feasibility calculations](feasibility.py) · [Training counts](feasibility.json)

The earlier catalogue had a nonempty artwork date on 59,618 objects and a nonempty artist field on 51,642. The release records dates as free text, including centuries and approximate ranges. A future predictor must freeze its normalization and compare the same representation across methods. Literal labels such as “No Known Copyright” and “No Copyright–United States” remain distinct from “Public Domain.” They fall in the other class for this specific declaration-recovery task. Both “Copyright Not Evaluated” and “Copyright Undetermined” are explicit observed declarations in the artificial-masking experiment; the pending-transition experiment treats them as the early eligibility states.

Both audit implementations read only training object documents, after excluding the two records used to inspect the schema. The museum documents a canonical bucket path for each ID. The later archive also contains thousands of noncanonical paths; the primary analysis uses valid canonical rows. Of 57,548 training IDs with valid object bodies at both locations, **14,437 had differing nonblank rights strings**. Among the 1,302 initially pending objects, 1,187 had conflicting later declarations. Excluding these leaves 61 still pending, 53 with another substantive declaration and only one with a Public Domain declaration. The export cannot identify a unique later declaration for conflicting records without resolving path provenance. The releases trace catalogue changes, with no independent legal adjudication.
